title: The Weight of Evidence
tagline: A koi is missing. A cat is framed. The board meets Friday.

beatrice.name: Beatrice
offline: I'm going to pretend I didn't hear that and wait for a better question. There are several right there.
Mm. Ask me something I can answer without leaving this radiator.
That's a question for a cat with more energy. Try another.

zeina.name: Zeina
offline: Wrong question, Listener. Try one that's going somewhere.
I don't answer that one. Ask me something useful.
Pass. You've got better questions than that.

hanako.name: Hanako
offline: The water is too murky for that question. Ask me another.
Bubbles. That is all I have for that one. Ask differently.
I don't know that. Ask me something a pond would know.

mortimer.name: Mortimer
offline: Shiny question, sweetheart, but I can't trade on it. Ask me another!
Mortimer doesn't know that one. Mortimer knows other things. Ask!
No deal on that, sweetheart. Try a different question.

emperor.name: Emperor
offline: That question is beneath me, and I am at the bottom of a bucket. Ask another.
I decline to answer, magnificently. Try again.
A koi of fourteen years does not dignify that. Ask me something else.

red_shadow.title: A red cat on the wall
red_shadow.note: Beatrice woke around 3 a.m. and saw a thin red cat on the back wall, watching the pond.

the_net.title: A gloved hand with a net
the_net.note: Hanako saw a torch beam, then a hand in a yellow rubber glove with a long pond net. Not a paw.

brushed_fur.title: The fur was planted
brushed_fur.note: The white fur on the pond's edge is dry, matted and smells of tumble-dryer: brushed out, not shed. Somebody put it there.

emperor_alive.title: Emperor may be alive
emperor_alive.note: Emperor was tipped into something that sloshed. Nobody carries dinner in a bucket of water. They carry merchandise.

beatrice_water.title: Beatrice and water
beatrice_water.note: Beatrice has not voluntarily touched water since the Bath of 2023. She could not fish if her dinner depended on it.

the_man.title: The man with the cooler
the_man.note: Zeina saw a hooded man in yellow gloves come out of the basement door, net Emperor into a blue cooler, then sprinkle white fluff on the pond's edge.

the_earring.title: Zeina's gold earring
the_earring.note: Zeina was on the wall to sell Mortimer the crow a gold earring she lifted from a balcony.

zeina_6c.title: Zeina was born here
zeina_6c.note: Zeina grew up in flat 6C. Three winters ago her family moved somewhere that 'doesn't allow pets' and left her behind.

earring_paid.title: Mortimer has been paid
earring_paid.note: Zeina dropped the gold earring into Mortimer's nest. It hurt her more than she let on.

the_van.title: Friday, 7 a.m., cash
the_van.note: Mortimer heard Gordon Pike, the superintendent, on the phone: Fenwick Aquatics collects the fish at the back gate, Friday 7 a.m., cash. 'The cat takes the blame.'

pike_debts.title: Pike's debts
pike_debts.note: Pike owes money to the men from the bookmaker's on the high street. His car was towed last month.

boiler_room.title: Pike's new routine
boiler_room.note: Since Wednesday Pike has made four trips to the boiler room with buckets of water and bags of ice. The boiler room hums like an aquarium.

coal_chute.title: The coal chute
coal_chute.note: Zeina spends winters behind the boiler, in secret. The old coal chute from the courtyard comes out right there.

abernathy_walk.title: 6:55, every morning
abernathy_walk.note: Mrs. Abernathy comes down to feed the koi at 6:55 sharp, singing Puccini. She would know Emperor's face anywhere.

the_plan.title: The plan
the_plan.note: When Pike wheels the tub out at seven: Zeina yowls from the wall to turn every head, and Beatrice sits on the tub. Pike cannot shift seven kilos of principle.

zeina_stays.title: A second cushion
zeina_stays.note: Zeina will stay. Not with Beatrice. Near Beatrice. There is a difference, she says, and it is very important.

crate_6c.title: Something in 6C
crate_6c.note: A crate with air holes and a padlock moves into 6C on Monday. Whatever is inside it asked Mortimer for Zeina by name.

scenes.title: Something Fishy

intro.text: At two minutes past six on a Thursday morning, Mrs. Abernathy of flat 2B stepped into the courtyard of the Marlowe building, looked into her koi pond, and screamed loud enough to set off a car alarm on the next street.
Emperor, her fourteen-year-old prize koi, a fish worth more than most of the cars on that street, was gone.

On the edge of the pond lay a damp clump of white fur. And six feet away, on the warm grate of the boiler vent, lay Beatrice of flat 4A. Round. White. Grey patches like a storm that had decided to stay. Damp paws.
Gordon Pike, the building superintendent, picked up the fur between two fingers as if it were a signed confession. There's your thief, he said. The board meets Friday. That cat goes to the farm.
I would like it noted that I have never in my life caught anything faster than a yoghurt lid.
Nobody noted it. Humans never do. But you can hear them, can't you? Somebody in this courtyard saw what happened last night. Ask.

scenes.objective: Find out what really happened at the pond last night. Talk to Beatrice and to Hanako, the koi left behind.
scenes.hint: Ask Beatrice what she saw or heard while she dozed by the pond. Ask Hanako whether it was really a cat that took Emperor.

outro.text: A red cat on the wall. A gloved hand with a net. Beatrice considered both facts the way she considered stairs: with dread, and a growing certainty that she would have to deal with them personally.
Right. The red one. She'll be on the roof. They always are. Six flights. If I die, tell 4A I loved the expensive tuna and merely tolerated him.

beatrice.greeting: Ah. A voice with no body. Either I'm finally going mad, or you're the first one round here with any sense. Ask your questions. Quickly. I'm due a nap in four minutes.

chips.a: Look at me. Really look. Do I strike you as a creature who goes into water, at night, for exercise? I have not voluntarily touched water since the Bath of 2023.
I drank from the pond. Carefully. I'm banned from the bathroom tap since the incident, and no, we will not be discussing the incident.

chips.q: Did anything wake you in the night?
chips.a: A clank, about three. I opened one eye. There was a cat on the back wall. Red, thin as a rumour, staring at the pond like it owed her money. Then I closed the eye. I'm a cat, darling, not a night watchman.

chips.q: Is that fur on the pond yours?
chips.a: It's white, so naturally everyone assumes. But smell it. Dry under the damp, matted, and it reeks of tumble-dryer. That's brushed fur, not shed fur. And my grooming brush went missing from the laundry room on Tuesday.

hanako.greeting: A voice. How novel. If you've come to apologise on behalf of the cat, you can save your breath. I have none to spare on you either.

chips.a: Eleven years. He is vain, he is loud, he sings at the moon. The pond is very quiet without him. I do not care for quiet.
That one? She drinks from my pond as if it might bite her. No. Cats come from the wall. This did not come from the wall.
A light first. A beam of torch, sweeping. Then a hand in a yellow rubber glove, and a long pole with a net. Cats do not wear gloves, dear. Not even the clever ones.
He went from the net into something that sloshed. A box of water. Nobody carries dinner in a bucket of water. They carry merchandise. So yes. I believe he is alive, and very annoyed.

scenes.title: The Red Cat

intro.text: It took Beatrice forty minutes to climb six flights of stairs. She stopped twice to rest, once to judge a moth, and once on the fifth floor landing to reconsider her entire life.
On the roof, the city hummed. On the rim of the old water tower sat a cat the colour of a struck match. Sleek, trim, and very, very still.
So you're the one they're sending to the farm. You're bigger than they said.
And you're the red shadow on the wall. You're smaller than I'd hoped. I was planning to sit on you.
Zeina. No collar. No flat. A reputation on every fire escape from here to the river. She does not tell strangers anything for free. But she is still here, which means she wants something too.

scenes.objective: Get Zeina to tell you what she saw from the wall at 3 a.m.
scenes.hint: Zeina won't volunteer anything. Tell her Beatrice saw her on the wall, or that Beatrice is going to the farm for it, and ask her straight what she saw.

outro.text: I didn't see his face. But Mortimer did. Mortimer sees everything that glitters, and that man was wearing a gold watch.
Zeina dropped off the water tower without a sound. Beatrice followed, with considerably more sound.

zeina.greeting: A voice in the dark that isn't a pigeon. Fine. You get three questions, and the first one was 'who are you', so you have two left.

chips.a: Zeina. No collar, no flat, no forwarding address. I do a bit of everything. Mostly I don't get caught.

chips.q: Why were you on the wall at three?
chips.a: Business. I had something to sell to a crow called Mortimer. A gold earring, if you must know. It fell off a balcony. Into my mouth. Gravity's funny like that.

chips.q: Beatrice goes to the farm for this. What did you see?
chips.a: Fine. Three oh five, the courtyard light clicks off. A man in a hood comes out of the basement door. Yellow rubber gloves, long net, blue cooler on a trolley. One scoop and your big orange fish is in the box. Then he sprinkles something white on the edge of the pond. Fluff. And he goes back the way he came.
Here and there. Mostly there. Next question.

beatrice.greeting: Six flights. Six. I want a medal, and then I want to lie down on the medal.

chips.q: How do we get her to talk?
chips.a: Pride. Look at her. That cat has never once been told she's the best thief on the block, and it's eating her alive. Tell her I'll be shipped off for her silence. She'll pretend she doesn't care. Watch her ears.
My heart is doing something I don't approve of, and I can see my breath. Ask me again after I've sat on something warm.

scenes.title: The Fence

intro.text: Mortimer's nest sat in the bones of the Marlowe's old television aerial like a crown that had been assembled by a magpie with a gambling problem. Bottle caps. Foil. Seven keys to nothing. A wedding ring nobody had reported.
Red! And you've brought a cloud. Sweetheart, I love what you've done with the place, the place being you. What are we buying tonight?
The man with the net. Three o'clock last night. You were on the bins.
I might have been. Information is shiny too, sweetheart. It just doesn't fit in the nest. What have you got for me?

scenes.objective: Mortimer knows who the man is. Find a way to pay him.
scenes.hint: Mortimer only deals in shiny things. Zeina has something gold on her. Ask her to pay him, then ask Mortimer again.

outro.text: Pike. Of course it's Pike. A man named after a fish, stealing a fish. It's practically a cry for help.
Seven in the morning. That's six hours. So where's the fish now?
I have an idea. Unfortunately, it involves the basement.

mortimer.greeting: Ooh, a voice from nowhere. Very exclusive. I'll do business with anybody, sweetheart, but nobody gets credit.

chips.q: Who was the man with the net?
chips.a: Oh, I know. I heard him on the telephone and everything. Lovely gold watch. But that's premium information, sweetheart, and premium costs. Something shiny. Something gold, ideally. I'm not fussy. I'm extremely fussy.

chips.q: The earring is yours. Now talk.
chips.a: Pleasure doing business. The man was Gordon Pike, your superintendent, gold watch and all. By the bins at twenty past three: Fenwick, it's Pike. I've got him. Friday seven a.m., back gate, cash. The cat takes the blame, the board meets at eight, everybody's happy. Everybody except the cat, I suppose.

chips.q: Why would anyone steal a fish?
chips.a: Money, sweetheart. It's always money. Our friend owes the gentlemen from the bookmaker's on the high street. They towed his car last month. I watched the whole thing. Best morning of my year.

zeina.greeting: Don't look at me like that. I know what he wants. I'm thinking about it.

chips.q: What can we pay him with?
chips.a: I've got the earring. It was going to be my winter. A crow's money buys a lot of warm doorways. Don't ask me for it. Ask me properly, or don't ask.
Fine. Fine. There. Gold, real, a little bit chewed. Happy, bird? Don't answer that.

scenes.title: The Laundry Room

intro.text: The Marlowe's laundry room, a quarter past one. The dryers were still warm from the night nurse in 3F, and lint turned slowly in the light like something thinking.
Beatrice settled onto the folding table as if she had been poured there and left to set.
You keep saying you have an idea.
I do. I'm thinking it slowly, so it doesn't get away.

scenes.objective: Work out where Pike is hiding Emperor, and how to get in.
scenes.hint: Beatrice has watched this building for six years: ask her about Pike's habits. Zeina knows the basement better than she admits: ask her how to get past a locked door.

outro.text: Two cats regarded the mouth of the coal chute. One of them fit.
Your face said it in italics.
It took eleven minutes, a great deal of breathing in, and one final push that Zeina would describe afterwards, with real respect, as structural.

beatrice.greeting: Don't let the shape fool you. This is the shape of a cat who has been paying attention for six years.

chips.a: Everyone thinks I'm lazy. I'm not lazy. I surveil. Six years of radiators and landings. Ask me about anyone in this building and I'll tell you when they eat, when they lie, and when they cry in the stairwell.

chips.q: So what has Pike been doing?
chips.a: That's the thing. Pike never comes down after six. Never. But since Wednesday he's been down here four times. Buckets from this sink. Ice from the corner shop. All of it through that door. And listen. Hear that hum? That's not the boiler. That's an aquarium pump. He's in there.

chips.q: Where did the fur come from?
chips.a: Look at the hook by the sink. My grooming brush lived there. Gone. And somebody's emptied the lint trap of dryer two, which was, frankly, mostly me.

zeina.greeting: If this is the part where you two bond, I'm going to go and stand somewhere else.

chips.q: Where do you sleep when it's cold?
chips.a: Somewhere warm. Somewhere nobody looks. Why, are you offering?

chips.q: How do we get past a locked door?
chips.a: You don't. Doors are for people with keys. There's a hatch by the courtyard bins, the old coal chute. Metal slide, straight down, and you come out behind the boiler. I've slept back there every winter for three years. Getting her through it, though. That's not a route. That's a construction project.

chips.q: Why do you stay near this building?
chips.a: I was born in 6C. Top floor, east side. They moved somewhere that doesn't allow pets. Three winters ago. I watched the van from the roof. That's the whole story, and you'll notice I'm not telling it twice.

scenes.title: The Boiler Room

intro.text: The boiler room was hot and red and breathing, like the inside of something large that had eaten recently.
Behind the boiler, in a blue plastic tub with an aquarium pump muttering to itself, floated fourteen years of orange and white self-regard.
Finally! Rescuers! Or assassins. Honestly, at this point I'd accept either, as long as somebody acknowledges that I have been kept in a bucket. A bucket! Me!
It's a tub.
It is a bucket with ambitions, madam, and so, evidently, are you.

scenes.objective: Five hours until the van. Make a plan that gets a human to see Emperor at 7 a.m.
scenes.hint: You need a human witness who would know Emperor on sight. Ask Emperor who comes down to the pond in the morning, and when. Then ask Beatrice what she wants to do about it.

outro.text: Let me be sure I understand. My rescue depends on a stray cat screaming, and a fat cat sitting down.
And she's very, very good at sitting down.

emperor.greeting: Oh good, another visitor. Do you know, I have been in this bucket for a day and nobody has once commented on my colouring.

chips.a: Physically? Untouched. Spiritually? I have been in a bucket. I have watched a man in rubber gloves eat a sandwich over me. Draw your own conclusions.

chips.q: What do you know about the handover?
chips.a: He talks to himself while he changes the ice. Quarter to seven, he wheels me out. Seven sharp, the back gate, a van. He keeps saying Fenwick like it's a prayer.

chips.q: Who comes to the pond in the morning?
chips.a: Mrs. Abernathy. Six fifty-five, every morning, rain or shine. She brings the good pellets and sings Puccini at us. Badly. With such feeling. She would know my face anywhere. She is the only human who has ever understood me.
Hanako is a deeply difficult fish. She corrects my singing. She takes the warm side of the pond. Tell her, if you see her, that the warm side is hers. Tell her nothing else. She'll understand.

beatrice.greeting: We will never speak of the coal chute. Is that clear? Good. Now. Let's ruin a man's morning.

chips.q: Can't we just push the tub out?
chips.a: Seven point two kilos of me versus forty litres of water and one very large ego. No. We need a human to see him. One who'd know that fish on sight. Ask his lordship who visits the pond.

Seven o'clock. Pike wheels the tub across the courtyard, past the pond, past Mrs. Abernathy singing Puccini at a widow. Zeina gets on the back wall and screams like the world is ending. Every head turns. And I sit on the lid. He can't lift it. He can't hide it. Something slides. And Mrs. Abernathy finds herself looking her fish in the face.

zeina.greeting: If anyone asks, I was never in this room and I have never helped anybody.

chips.a: I'm not. I'm helping the fish. The fish is very rich. Next question.
Because somebody once got sent away from this building for nothing, and nobody stopped the van. That's why. Don't make it a thing.
Can I be loud. I once made a man on the fourth floor of the building across the road call the police on a car alarm. It was me. I was the car alarm.

scenes.title: Seven A.M.

intro.text: Six fifty-eight, Friday. The back gate creaked. In the lane a white van idled, Fenwick Aquatics stencilled on its side, and underneath, in smaller letters, the word discreet.
Gordon Pike wheeled a blue tub across the courtyard with the careful, casual air of a man who has rehearsed being casual. At the pond, Mrs. Abernathy was singing Puccini, badly, to a widow.
From the top of the back wall came a yowl so loud and so filthy it should have needed a licence. Every head in the courtyard turned.
And Beatrice, all seven point two kilograms of her, launched herself off the boiler grate in what witnesses would later describe as a gallop, and landed on the lid of the tub.
Pike pulled. The tub did not move. Beatrice did not move. Beatrice had been not moving, professionally, for six years.
The lid slid an inch. Water slopped. And an orange and white face, fourteen years old and incandescent with rage, rose into the gap and looked Mrs. Abernathy dead in the eye.

What followed involved a garden hose, two neighbours with phones, and the word Gordon, screamed in a register normally reserved for opera. By eight o'clock, the board meeting had a new agenda item. It was not Beatrice.

scenes.objective: The case is closed. Talk to your new friends. Ask Zeina what she'll do now, and find out why Mortimer has come.
scenes.hint: Ask Zeina whether she's staying. Ask Mortimer what news he's brought.

outro.text: And so the fat cat and the thin cat sat on the warm grate together, not touching, which for cats is practically a wedding.
Above them, on the sixth floor, in the empty flat called 6C, something in a crate with air holes shifted its weight, and listened.

beatrice.greeting: Salmon. A whole tin. Mrs. Abernathy called me a hero and I let her. Ask me anything. I'm in an expansive mood. Physically and spiritually.

chips.q: How does it feel to be a hero?
chips.a: Heavy. Which is, it turns out, the whole point. Six years everyone said I just sat there. I did just sit there. At exactly the right moment.

chips.q: Are you and Zeina friends now?
chips.a: Friends is a strong word. We are two cats who have been through a coal chute together. Well. One of us went through it. One of us was posted. And there may be a second cushion by my radiator. For no reason. My person bought it. I didn't ask him to. I sat on the shop page until he did.

zeina.greeting: Don't. I can see you're going to say something nice. Don't.

chips.a: I know. I've been saving it. You only get one of those a life, and I spent mine on a fish I've never met and a cat who sat on me twice in the chute.

Mrs. Abernathy has started leaving a bowl on her balcony. And someone in 4A has bought a cushion they have no use for. So, yes. I'm staying. Not with her. Near her. There's a difference, and it's very important.

mortimer.greeting: Bravo, bravo. Best thing I've seen since the car got towed. And I've brought you something, sweetheart. Free of charge. That should worry you.

chips.a: Free gossip, sweetheart, and you know I never do free. Ask me about 6C.

Somebody's moving in Monday. Furniture's not up yet, but the first thing the movers carried up was a crate. Air holes. A padlock. Not on any lease, I'd bet my nest on it. And last night, through the air holes, it asked me for her. For Red. By name.

next.title: Episode 2: The Tenant in 6C
next.teaser: Something in a padlocked crate knows Zeina's name. Zeina's old flat has a new occupant. And Beatrice has just discovered she enjoys being right.
